The natural gas feedstock (Stream 1) for the plant is sourced from a pipeline. The natural gas for the reforming section is sent to a sulfur guard unit that uses a ZnO catalyst to remove methanethiol, which can poison the reforming catalysts. Next, the desulfurized natural gas (Stream 2) is mixed with steam (Stream 3) at a steam-to-carbon molar ratio of 2.61. The mixture is sent to the primary reformer where hydrocarbons are reformed over a nickel oxide catalyst to produce a partially-reformed gas stream (Stream 4). Energy to drive the reforming reactions is provided by firing a mixture of ambient air (Stream 5) and the supplemental fuel natural gas (Stream 6) blended with the retentate gas from the H membrane on the outside of the 2 reformer reactor tubes. Ambient air (Stream 7) is then added to the secondary reformer to further convert methane through reaction with O and to add N to the system so that 3.0 is the 2 2 hydrogen-to-nitrogen ratio of the stream entering the ammonia synthesis loop. The secondary reformer completes the reforming process to produce syngas. The hot syngas (Stream 8) is sent to syngas coolers, which cool the syngas from 982 °C (1,800 °F) to 204 °C (400 °F) while producing steam. The cooled syngas (Stream 9) is then sent through a series of three water gas shift reactors in which carbon monoxide and water are converted to additional H and CO . Carbon oxides and water need to be removed prior to the ammonia 2 2 synthesis loop due to their ability to poison the catalyst. The shifted syngas (Stream 10) is sent to the Shell ADIP-Ultra pre-combustion CO capture system that removes 99 percent of the CO 2 2 in the syngas. The ADIP-Ultra unit produces low-pressure (Stream 11) and medium-pressure (Stream 12) streams containing CO that are sent to CO compression and drying in capture 2 2 cases. The remaining carbon oxides in the gas stream (Stream 13) are converted to methane in the methanation reactor and the water produced from the methanation reaction is removed from the gas stream as well.
